abstract.t: A profile of RFC 8017 for the signing functions of nish/crypto/rsa-sign: RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256 and MGF1 with SHA-256, the scheme TLS 1.3 names rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 (RFC 8446 Section 4.2.3), over the RSASP1 primitive with a private key of 2048 to 4096 bits. Every requirement quotes RFC 8017, the main source, or RFC 8446; every binding sentence of RFC 8017 (MUST, MUST NOT, SHALL, SHALL NOT, REQUIRED) is tested or excluded here.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

nish/crypto/rsa-sign signs with RSASSA-PSS (RFC 8017 Section 8.1.1), its encoding EMSA-PSS (Section 9.1.1) with Hash SHA-256 and MGF MGF1 with SHA-256 (Section B.2.1), so hLen is 32, over RSASP1 in the first form (n, d) of the private key (Section 5.2.1). rsaParsePrivateKey reads a DER RSAPrivateKey (Section A.1.2) from der[start, end) and returns the key as a Secret: the modulus n, the private exponent d and the public exponent e, each as k big-endian octets, where k is the octet length of n, in that order, 3k octets in all. It refuses, with null, anything but a version 0 key whose n is odd and of 2048 to 4096 bits, whose e is odd and in [3, 2^32), and whose d is in (0, n). The properties see the key as bytes.

rsaSignRaw(key, m) is RSASP1: m is k octets, and the result is m^d mod n as k octets, or null when m is not k octets or not below n. It checks its result by raising it to the third slot, e, so the key with its second and third slots swapped, concat(n, concat(e, d)), computes s^e mod n, the verification primitive RSAVP1 (Section 5.2.2). The properties recover the encoded message of a signature that way and check every field of it.

rsaSignPssSha256Salted(key, msg, salt) signs msg with the salt it is given, so sLen is the salt's length; rsaSignPssSha256(key, msg) signs with a 32-octet salt, as TLS 1.3 asks, which it derives itself. Both return the k-octet signature, or null.
Out of scope: RsaSignScratch, the reusable scratch of rsaSignPssSha256Into and rsaSignPssSha256SaltedInto, a class and not a function

Out of scope: rsaSignPssSha256Into, the same signature as rsaSignPssSha256 written into a caller's array through an RsaSignScratch, held by tests/link/crypto_rsa_sign; its first parameter is the class RsaSignScratch, which vector 0.6.0 refuses in a ts-interface block ("RsaSignScratch is not a ts-interface type; use u8[], string, boolean, i8, i16, i32, i64, u8, u16, u32, u64, f64, Secret<u8[]>, u16[], u32[], u64[], each optionally | null"), and it answers a boolean where an /* out CAP */ write returns the end offset
Out of scope: rsaSignPssSha256SaltedInto, the same signature as rsaSignPssSha256Salted written into a caller's array through an RsaSignScratch, for the reasons rsaSignPssSha256Into is
Out of scope: RSA_SIGN_MIN_BITS, an i32 constant a vector or property cannot call; P-KEY-2048 holds the smallest modulus accepted
Out of scope: RSA_SIGN_MAX_BITS, an i32 constant a vector or property cannot call; P-KEY-4096 holds the largest modulus accepted

section.name: Out of Scope
section.t: RFC 8017 prints no RSASSA-PSS signature, so this spec has no vector. The known answers of P-KAT-2048, P-KAT-2049 and P-KAT-4096 were computed for this spec by an independent implementation of Sections 8.1.1, 9.1.1 and B.2.1 over Python's integers, and each signature was checked with the RSASSA-PSS verification of the Python cryptography package. The three keys were made for this spec: the 2048- and 4096-bit keys by OpenSSL, and the 2049-bit key, whose encoded message is one octet shorter than k, from two 1025-bit primes, since OpenSSL rounds the size of a key it generates. None of them signs anything outside these tests.

Verification is not a property here: rsaVerifyPss in nish/crypto/rsa takes the class RsaPublicKey, which vector 0.6.0 refuses in a ts-interface block. The properties run RSAVP1 through rsaSignRaw instead, under the swapped key, and check the encoded message field by field, which is what EMSA-PSS-VERIFY (Section 9.1.2) checks.

The salt of rsaSignPssSha256 is not random (Section 9.1.1 step 4): it is derived from the private key and the message, so the signature is the same for the same key and message. Its derivation is an implementation choice that RFC 8017 does not constrain, so no property fixes it; P-TLS-SALT holds that the salt it uses is 32 octets and that the signature is the one rsaSignPssSha256Salted makes with that salt.

The message-too-long errors (Section 8.1.1 step 1 and Section 9.1.1 step 1) need a message of 2^61 octets, and MGF1's mask-too-long error (Section B.2.1 step 1) a mask of 2^37 octets; neither can be built, so neither is tested. RSASP1's second form (p, q, dP, dQ, qInv) is not used: the key is kept as (n, d), and the result is the same integer.

section.name: Properties

abstract.t: This document provides recommendations for the implementation of public-key cryptography based on the RSA algorithm, covering cryptographic primitives, encryption schemes, signature schemes with appendix, and ASN.1 syntax for representing keys and for identifying the schemes.
This document represents a republication of PKCS #1 v2.2 from RSA Laboratories' Public-Key Cryptography Standards (PKCS) series. By publishing this RFC, change control is transferred to the IETF.

front.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

abstract.t: This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol. TLS allows client/server applications to communicate over the Internet in a way that is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery.
This document updates RFCs 5705 and 6066, and obsoletes RFCs 5077, 5246, and 6961. This document also specifies new requirements for TLS 1.2 implementations.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.
